theme_scores.justification: Lines 11-16 describe what verification steps will be required but offer no data, research or comparable-policy evidence for why this particular verification route (NI number, passport, attestation) was chosen over alternatives.

The claim that the existing two-attestation limit 'is designed to put a limit on any potentially fraudulent applications' and the move to align overseas limits with domestic ones is justified only by an appeal to consistency, not by any fraud statistics or evaluation, and Reference 4 merely defines a time period rather than supplying evidence.

Lines 17-20 set out a cascade of verification methods (register check, documentary evidence, attestation) with no cited data, trial, or comparable case to justify why this sequence of checks is adequate or preferable to alternatives.

The intent 'to increase the numbers of overseas electors who renew annually' (line 25) and the mandatory-reminder policy are asserted without any evidence (e.g. renewal/lapse rates, pilot results) that reminders or a 12-month cycle achieve this, and Reference 5 only clarifies a date definition.
Describes categories and franchise limits with no evidence cited for why these boundaries were set.
States channels (GOV.UK, paper, telephone) with Reference 3 being only a URL to the service itself, not evidence of its effectiveness or uptake.
Restates existing franchise rules with no supporting evidence for the implementation choice.
Mentions funding for EROs 'in accordance with the new burdens doctrine' with no figures, estimates or source given.

reasoning: The core themes - identity verification, attestation limits, address verification, and renewal/duration - together carry the bulk of the implementation argument, and none of them cite empirical evidence for the chosen delivery method. They are almost entirely procedural description: lines 11-20 lay out a sequence of checks (NI number, passport, attestation, register check) and lines 22-25 describe a 12-month renewal cycle with mandatory reminders, but no statistic, research finding, consultation result, or comparable-policy experience is offered to justify why these specific thresholds, time limits, or verification chains were selected over alternatives. The closest the document comes to reasoning is the attestation theme's claim that the current unlimited overseas attestation rule 'is inconsistent' with the domestic two-per-elector limit (supporting lines near Reference 4) - but this is an internal consistency argument, not evidence of effect, and Reference 4 only defines a date range. The non-core themes (eligibility categories, application channels, franchise types) are similarly evidence-free, including Reference 3's bare link to gov.uk. Costs are mentioned only vaguely ('funding...in accordance with the new burdens doctrine') with no figures. Because no theme, core or otherwise, reaches even level 1 - evidence mentioned with explanation of how it was used - the section as a whole stays at 0. To reach level 1, the document would need to show, for example, data on fraud rates under the current attestation system, renewal/lapse statistics justifying mandatory reminders, or findings from a comparable jurisdiction's overseas registration process.
